question.text: Fund CAS holds a 12% convertible bond (face INR 1 crore, conversion ratio 25:1 at INR 40 effective price) and a short position of 50,000 equity shares at INR 40. After 1 year, the EQUITY price FALLS to INR 35 and the bond trades at INR 1,020. Under Convertible Arbitrage, which action best preserves gains?

answer.text: Convert the bonds into equity and cover the short with the converted shares
Double the short position to hedge the bond's upside
Hold the bond (earn coupon) and close the short at the lower price of INR 35, booking gain on the short leg
Sell the bond at INR 1,020 and close the short at INR 35

explanation.text: The Logic: Per the AIF Managers workbook on Convertible Arbitrage (pp. 277-279), when the equity share price falls, the fund benefits from the short position and continues to earn fixed income on the convertible security. The source explicitly states that the fund would not convert if the price decreased and would square off the short position with gain, while continuing to hold the bond and receive coupons. With the equity at INR 35 versus the original INR 40, closing the 50,000-share short books a gain of INR 5 per share, and the bond is retained for ongoing coupon income. The Trap: Option A (converting during a price fall) is the wrong branch of the strategy because the source says the fund would not convert if the price decreased. Option B (doubling the short) adds directional risk rather than preserving the arbitrage. Option D prematurely sells the bond, forfeiting future coupon income and the embedded conversion optionality that the source describes. Note: Convertible arbitrage as described on pp. 277-279 has two clearly defined branches: if the equity price rises, convert and deliver to cover the short; if the equity price falls, do not convert and instead square off the short with gain while continuing to earn coupons on the bond.
